job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a master's in robotics at Calder Institute, and I live in a student house with a garage we've turned into a workshop. My day is lectures in the morning, then the lab where I'm building a gripper for picking soft fruit, then evenings on a side project, a small app that helps local cafes forecast how much milk to order. My bachelor's was mechatronics, which is a mix of mechanical, electrical and software. I did one internship at a warehouse robotics firm and one at a packaging company. I use AI tools all day, for code, for emails, even for planning my week, and what wears me out is when I take on too many things at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool and not a miracle. At work I'd say let's use it where it saves hours and drop it where it doesn't. To friends I'd say I told you so, a little, and then offer to help them set up the ones that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is fine for me. I'd still finish the master's, I'd still find work in robotics or automation, and I'd keep my side project running. If the hype fades, people who are good at making tools actually useful will do well, and I'm one of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a job at a robotics or automation firm, and keep the cafe app going on weekends. I'd put a bit of money into the app, like a proper server. And I'd go to a couple of trade shows to meet people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still work on the side project in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's what keeps me learning. The cafes pay about thirty a month each, and I've got six of them. It's not a business yet, but it's a proof I can ship something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overload, honestly. I take on a project, then another, and then fall behind on both. My housemate Priya is the one who tells me to cut something, and she's usually right.

I'd offer to help friends set up the tools that **actually work**.
think: A plateau is **fine** for me, since people who make tools useful do well.
My own risk is **overload**, taking on too many things at once.
do: Finish the master's and take a job at a **robotics or automation** firm.
Keep the **cafe app** running on weekends and pay for a proper server.
feel: **Calm**; it's a world he knows how to work in.

fieldNote: His **calm** is built on skill and a side project that already earns something.

Treats a plateau as a place where tool-makers win.

steps.text: Finish the robotics master's at Calder Institute
Apply to robotics and automation firms for the autumn
Keep the cafe milk-forecasting app running on weekends
Rent a proper server for the app from my savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving and we should ride it. At work I'd propose a pilot, one small task each team gives to software, then measure. To friends I'd say learn to ask better questions of the tools, because that's the new skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in the zone where I benefit and risk at once. Coding and planning get faster, so a firm needs fewer juniors for the same output. But robots in hands-on work come slower, and somebody has to build and fix them, which is my field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch my cafe app to a bigger chain as a pilot and see if it can grow. I'd sharpen the robotics side so I'm the one who understands the physical machine as well as the software. And I'd network at two trade shows a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I like being on the front of the wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the wave goes over you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be annoyed but not ruined. I've got money, no debt and parents who'd give me a room. I'd also have a few small projects, so no single one breaks me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Nadia, who does data entry for an insurance firm. Her work is routine screen tasks, and I've told her to learn some of the tools, but her manager doesn't allow it. I'd feel bad if she got cut first.

say: I'd say it's moving and we should **ride it**, starting with small pilots.
I'd tell friends to learn to **ask better questions** of the tools.
think: I benefit and risk at once: **juniors** get fewer, but robots still need building and fixing.
A few small projects mean no single one can **break me**.
do: Pitch the cafe app to a **bigger chain** as a pilot.
Sharpen my **robotics side** and go to two trade shows a year.
feel: **Calm** and a little excited to be near the front of the wave.
S1.quote: I'd be annoyed but not ruined. I've got money, no debt and parents who'd give me a room.
fieldNote: Adaptability shows as **diversification**: several small projects instead of one job.
Honest that his **cushion** protects him, and worries about his cousin Nadia.
Sees a role at the border of software and physical machines.

steps.text: Pitch the cafe app to a bigger chain as a pilot
Use AI tools daily and write down which prompts work
Take a hands-on robot maintenance course during the master's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's wild, and fast, and we're not ready. I'd say governments have to act within months, with income support and clear rules. And I'd say I'm still going to use every tool I can, because refusing doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the first one that rattles me. Thinking AI does almost any desk job by 2028, and robots do hands-on work as well as people 3 years later, so my master's is in the one field that is next to be taken. I'd have maybe five years where my skills are scarce, and then not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the cafe app and look for a few more small customers, since it's mine and not an employer's. I'd get a job at a robotics firm as early as possible, so I'm paid while I learn. And I'd put a chunk of savings into shares in the companies making the machines, which sounds cynical but is protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a streak of fear. It feels like building the thing that replaces you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a contradiction, working on robots while worried about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about it. If I don't build them, someone else will, and I'd rather be in the room. But I can't say I'm fully comfortable, and I'd tell a friend that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya, your housemate, that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we should stay in this house another year and keep the garage, because it's cheap and we can work. She'd say I'm hiding in the workshop, and she'd probably be right. We'd end up ordering pizza and arguing about who gets which part of the gripper.

say: I'd say it's **wild** and fast, and governments must act in months.
I'd say I'll still use every tool I can, because **refusing** helps nobody.
think: My master's is in the field **next in line**, so my skills might be scarce for only about five years.
It feels like **building the thing** that replaces me.
do: Push the cafe app to find a few more small **customers**.
Take a robotics job early and put part of my savings in **machine-making** companies.
S2.quote: If I don't build them, someone else will, and I'd rather be in the room.
fieldNote: He admits the **contradiction** of building robots he fears.
Strong cushion keeps him **uneasy** rather than anxious.
Hedges by owning shares in the machine makers.

steps.text: Look for a few more small cafe customers for the app
Take a robotics job as early as possible
Put a chunk of savings into shares of robot makers
Keep using the best AI coding tools every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a proper chance to act, so let's act. I'd tell my firm to set a training budget now. And I'd tell friends to start a side project, because those become more useful when everything's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. By 2031 I'd be 29, with a few years in a robotics firm and a side business, and 2034 is when hands-on robots arrive for real. I'd be at the right place for the second half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a job in robot installation, and keep building the app into something I could sell. I'd save a third of my pay and invest some of it. And I'd start learning a trade-like skill, such as hydraulics, so I know how things work when the software fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a game I like playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you being calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year of silence, honestly. If I applied to twenty robotics firms and heard nothing, I'd get anxious fast. Companies are hiring now, but they could freeze when they see what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the five-year picture compare with the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between a sprint and a long hike. I'd still be working hard, but I'd get to pick the route. With two years I'd grab every job and project, but with five I'd choose the ones that grow.

say: Five years is a **proper chance** to act, so set a training budget now.
I'd tell friends to start a **side project**, which gets more useful in times of change.
think: I'd feel good: at 29 I'd have robotics and **business** experience, right for the second half.
Hands-on robots arrive in **2034**, so I'd be in the right place.
do: Take a **robot installation** job and build the app into something I can sell.
Save a **third of my pay**, invest some, and learn hydraulics.

steps.text: Take a robot installation job after the master's
Build the cafe app into something I could sell
Save a third of my pay each month
Invest part of my savings in index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to prepare, and the people who use it well will pull ahead. I'd tell friends to try a new tool every month. And I'd tell the council to teach it in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel excited. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe running my own small company, with ten years of robotics behind me. I'd also worry I'd get too relaxed and not notice the date sneaking up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at a robotics firm for a few years and then leave to start something of my own. I'd keep building small tools that solve real problems. And I'd pay down any debt, buy a flat and hold some cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. A decade is a lot of experiments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own company make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably tools that help small firms use robots without needing a team of engineers. Think of a bakery that wants a robot to pack boxes. I've seen what a good small tool does to a cafe, and the same thing could work in a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister, who's sixteen, to learn the tools now and to also learn one real-world skill, like cooking or electrics. Nobody knows what the future needs, but a person who can do both is hard to leave behind.

say: Ten years is **long** to prepare, and people who use it well will pull ahead.
I'd tell friends to try **a new tool** every month.
think: I'd feel excited: at 34 I might run my **own small company**.

Pay down any debt, buy a **flat** and hold some cash.

S4.quote: I'd tell my sister, who's sixteen, to learn the tools now and to also learn one real-world skill, like cooking or electrics.
fieldNote: A decade lets him think like a **founder**, with small robot tools for bakeries and similar firms.

steps.text: Work at a robotics firm for three or four years
Build simple robot packing tools for small bakeries
Keep the cafe app as a small second income
Pay off any debt and hold cash while buying a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one. Everything lines up badly for me there: my field is the next to be taken, there's no time to build a company, and a lot of people I know would be caught flat. What would help is quick income support, honest information about which skills last, and rules so a few companies don't own the whole thing. I'd also like a mentor who's seen a change like this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I come across as relaxed, but the relaxed part is learned. I tell myself small projects keep me safe, and I know that's partly a story. If someone asked me in 2028 whether I'm okay, I'd probably say no, and I'd want a person to say that's fair.

headlineQuote: I've seen what a good small tool does to a cafe, and the same thing could work in a factory.
portrait: Hassan is 24, doing a **master's** in robotics at Calder Institute and living in a student house with a workshop garage.
He is a pragmatic centrist, curious, takes risks and uses **AI tools daily**.
He keeps several small projects going, including a cafe forecasting app, so no single one can **break** him.
Only the 2028 picture truly unsettles him, since his own field of robotics is **next in line**.
He plans to build simple robot tools for small firms.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because robotics is the next field taken and there's no time to build a company.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **income support** and honest information about which skills last.
Rules that stop a few firms owning everything, plus a **mentor** who has seen change like this.
